subject: Archaeology
title: The Antikythera Shipwreck
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Antikythera Shipwreck.

hook.text: Greek sponge divers found a Roman shipwreck in 1900 that contained the world's first known analog computer.

buildup.text: The ship sank around 60 BCE near Antikythera island, carrying bronze statues, jewelry, glassware, and coins.

discovery.text: Among the corroded lumps was a gear mechanism with over 30 bronze wheels — it predicted eclipses and planetary positions.

twist.text: Nothing this complex appeared again for 1,400 years. The technology was lost when Rome fell and was not reinvented.

climax.text: X-ray imaging in 2006 revealed inscriptions and gear teeth. The full device is now digitally reconstructed.

punchline.text: Ancient Greeks built a computer. The sea hid it for 2,000 years.

quiz.question: What was the Antikythera Mechanism used for?
options: Navigating ships across the open Mediterranean
Predicting eclipses and tracking planetary positions
Calculating taxes owed to the Roman Senate

details.summary: The Antikythera shipwreck, discovered off Greece in 1900, yielded the Antikythera mechanism — an ancient Greek analogue computer for predicting astronomical events. The wreck also contained bronze statues, jewelry, and glassware, making it the richest ancient shipwreck ever found.
details.whyItMatters: The Antikythera mechanism rewrote our understanding of ancient technology. A device this complex was not supposed to exist for another thousand years, proving that ancient Greeks achieved a level of mechanical engineering previously thought.
takeaways: The Antikythera wreck was discovered off Greece in 1900
It yielded an ancient analogue computer for astronomical prediction
The mechanism proved Greek engineering was far more advanced than assumed

faq.question: What exactly does the Antikythera mechanism do?
faq.answer: It predicted solar and lunar eclipses, tracked the movements of the five known planets, and calculated dates for the Olympic Games. Using a system of at least 30 meshing bronze gears, it could model astronomical cycles with remarkable accuracy — essentially a 2,100-year-old computer.

faq.question: Why is the Antikythera wreck still being explored?
faq.answer: Modern technology reveals far more than 1900s sponge divers could recover. Recent expeditions using rebreathers and robotic equipment have found new bronze statue fragments, an intact skeleton for DNA analysis, and additional ship components in deeper sections of the wreck site.
